label: 1v
quote: Ausserdem ist wahr- scheinlich die Frage so zu beantworten, dass zunächst ein Integral beliebig aus- gewählt werden kann, wodurch eine Konstante da ist; sodann bilde man die Differentialgl. mit einer Unbekannten weniger (also die La- grange'sche Gl. für das entsprechende [-$\mathfrak{E}$-] Jacobische Variationsproblem) und von dieser wähle man nun das 2te Integral beliebig etc.
english: Moreover, the question is probably to be answered thus: first an integral can be chosen arbitrarily, whereby one constant is present; then one forms the differential equation with one fewer unknown (i.e. the Lagrange equation for the corresponding Jacobi variational problem), and from this one now chooses the 2nd integral arbitrarily, etc.
topic: The page derives a mean cohesive force from shifted electron distances, poses a Hamilton–Jacobi question about characterizing two-parameter families of solutions of intermediate first-order differential equations belonging to a given field, and notes the eigenvalue behaviour of the Hermite-type equation $y''-2xy'+2ny=0$.

triage.modern_statement: Take a variational problem ∫F(x,y,z,y',z')dx with two unknown functions y(x), z(x). Its Euler–Lagrange equations form a second-order system. Hilbert asks which 2-parameter families of solutions, written as first-order 'intermediate' systems y'=p(x,y,z), z'=q(x,y,z), make up a field. In modern terms this is a Mayer field: the slope functions (p,q) come from a solution S of the Hamilton–Jacobi equation, so the Hilbert invariant integral does not depend on the path. Hilbert's conjectured construction works one step at a time. First choose one first integral arbitrarily, which fixes one constant. Then use it to reduce the problem to an Euler–Lagrange equation in one fewer unknown, which he calls the Lagrange equation of the associated 'Jacobi' variational problem. Then choose the second integral of that reduced problem arbitrarily, and so on.
triage.answered_by: The general question of which families of extremals form a field has a standard classical answer. A field 'belongs to' a family of hypersurfaces S = const (a Mayer field) exactly when the Lagrange brackets of the field's parameters all vanish. Equivalently, certain integrability conditions hold, and these are made explicit in Carathéodory's Hamilton–Jacobi approach to the calculus of variations (his 1935 textbook). The two-unknown setting itself, with slope functions p(x,y,z) and q(x,y,z), is the one Hilbert treated in Problem 23 of his 1900 list, building on Kneser's field construction. I found no source that discusses or confirms Hilbert's specific step-by-step reduction (choose one integral, reduce to a Jacobi-type problem, choose the next), so I cannot say whether it was ever proved or published as stated.

evidence.claim: Problem 23 of Hilbert's 1900 list sets up a first-order differential equation for functions p and q of the three variables x, y, z. It also notes that Kneser builds, for any simple family of integral curves, a solution of a generalized Jacobi–Hamilton equation. This is the setting of the diary note.

A field belongs to a family of hypersurfaces if and only if the Lagrange brackets of the field's parameters vanish. This is the standard criterion for when a family of extremals forms a (Mayer) field.

An extremal can be embedded in a whole field of extremals (a Mayer field) only if certain integrability conditions hold. Carathéodory's formulation shows how these conditions relate to the Euler–Lagrange equations.
Hilbert's 23rd problem is not a specific problem. It is a general call to develop the calculus of variations further, so this note is not itself one of Hilbert's published problems.

triage.why: The note is a speculative remark about how to answer a structural question in Weierstrass–Kneser–Hilbert field theory for problems with two unknown functions. That question has a standard classical answer, now part of the textbook theory: a family is a field when its Lagrange brackets vanish, equivalently when it is generated by a Hamilton–Jacobi solution, and it fits Carathéodory's framework. It is not a separate Hilbert problem, although it is closely related to the material in Problem 23. I could not tie Hilbert's particular step-by-step procedure to any later source, and my search was cut short by the tool limit. So 'solved' refers to the underlying question, not to his exact conjectured method, and confidence is low.
